1 big thing: Early voting surges in key states
 
People hold signs directing voters to a polling place Wednesday in Minneapolis. Photo: Stephen Maturen/Getty Images

This year's early voting is significantly outpacing the last midterm elections, according to an Associated Press analysis of voting data five days before Election Day.

  • More than 43 million Americans have voted early in person or returned mail-in ballots — nearly 10 million more than in 2022.
  • The figures cover 47 states and D.C., compared with 48 states and D.C. four years ago.

🏛️ There have been particularly sharp increases in states hosting big competitive races.

  • In Texas, where voters are deciding closely watched Senate, House and governor's races, more than 6.3 million people voted early as of Wednesday.
  • That's compared with 4.2 million at the same point four years ago, a 50% increase.
Candidates' signs outside a polling place in Houston on Oct. 19. Photo: Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

🗳️ Early voting has also increased more than 30% from the same point four years ago in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas.

  • In South Carolina, where voters are choosing a successor to the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, early voting is up 83%.

Between the lines: In states that provide party affiliation data, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans have voted early.

  • Those figures don't account for all early voters nationwide, or indicate which candidates received their votes.

2. 🗳️ Pope makes voting history
 
Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photo via Getty Images

Pope Leo XIV has voted in the Illinois midterm elections using a mail-in ballot, Axios' Josephine Walker reports.

  • That makes him the first sitting pope to vote in a U.S. election.

⛪️ The Holy See Press Office said in a statement that Leo "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so" and that "in keeping with this long-standing practice of civic participation, he has submitted his mail-in ballot in Chicago."

  • The statement added that Leo believes "in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes."

🫏🐘 Leo has voted in both Democratic and Republican primaries over the last two decades.

4. ⏰ 1 for the road: Hacking the time change
 
Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios

A few small tweaks can ease this weekend's "fall back" to standard time, Renske Lok, a circadian biologist at the University of Colorado Boulder, tells Axios Denver's Alayna Alvarez.

Here's how to hack it:

  • 🛌 Start tonight. Shift your bedtime and wake-up time back by 10–12 minutes a day to give your internal clock a head start.
  • 👶 Parents, beware. Babies and kids don't understand the shift to standard time, so a 6 a.m. wake-up call could become 5 a.m.
  • 💤 Don't count on bonus sleep. Data from Oura users shows that they slept less overall the week after the 2024 fall time change, despite gaining an hour.
  • ☀️ Chase the morning sun. Getting outside early helps your body adjust.
